Adventured
ad-VEN-churd
v. (risked, ventured; of Gideon, who adventured his life far and was repaid by the murder of his sons)
From Old French aventure, from Latin adventurus, about to happen. At Judges 9:17 it renders Hebrew shalak, to cast or fling — literally, he flung his life out in front of him.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Jotham is standing on the top of mount Gerizim shouting down at the men of Shechem who have just crowned his half-brother Abimelech after murdering seventy of his brothers on one stone. He reminds them what their king's father did for them: For my father fought for you, and adventured his life far, and delivered you out of the hand of Midian. The Hebrew verb is the one for casting or flinging — Gideon threw his life out ahead of him, three hundred men against a host lying along the valley like grasshoppers for multitude. And this is what the men of Shechem paid back.

The word describes the same virtue Acts commends in Barnabas and Paul, and Judges 9 supplies the other half of the picture: risk taken faithfully is not always met with gratitude, and often the reckoning comes a generation late. David did put his life in his hand, and slew the Philistine, and the LORD wrought a great salvation for all Israel, and Jonathan has to remind Saul of it while Saul is trying to kill him. Jotham's parable of the trees ends in a curse that took three years to come true, and it came true exactly. The believer who has adventured something for God and been ill repaid is in old company, and the book of Judges does not tell him the accounting has been cancelled — only that it is not his to make.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): risked; hazarded; ventured; exposed to danger or loss.

expand to see more

ADVENTURED, pp. Risked; hazarded; put to hazard.

ADVENTURE, v.t. To risk or hazard; to venture; to dare.

DELIVER, v.t. To free; to release, as from restraint; to set at liberty; to rescue.

REQUITE, v.t. To repay; to return an equivalent, in a good or bad sense.

PARABLE, n. A fable or allegorical relation or representation of something real in life or nature.

Key Scripture

Judges 9:17 — "(For my father fought for you, and adventured his life far, and delivered you out of the hand of Midian:"

1 Samuel 19:5 — "For he did put his life in his hand, and slew the Philistine, and the LORD wrought a great salvation for all Israel: thou sawest it, and didst rejoice: wherefore then wilt thou sin against innocent blood, to slay David without a cause?"

Acts 15:26 — "Men that have hazarded their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ."

Philippians 2:30 — "Because for the work of Christ he was nigh unto death, not regarding his life, to supply your lack of service toward me."

Modern Corruption

Faithful risk is expected to be rewarded in this life, and when it is not, the believer concludes that God did not see it; Judges 9 says the accounting is real and slow.

expand to see more

Jotham's speech is the sharpest statement in Scripture of a grievance every generation feels: a man spent himself for people who forgot it and then destroyed his house. The chapter does not answer with sentiment. It answers with a verdict — God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of Shechem — and with an account settled three years later, when a woman cast a piece of millstone from a tower and broke Abimelech's skull. The narrator states the theology plainly: Thus God rendered the wickedness of Abimelech, which he did unto his father, in slaying his seventy brethren.

The pastoral use is not vindictiveness but patience. A believer who has adventured something real — a reputation, a livelihood, a friendship — and watched it go unacknowledged is tempted to conclude either that the risk was foolish or that God was inattentive. Judges 9 rules out both. The accounting is real, it is God's, and its timing is not the aggrieved man's to set. Paul says the same in a quieter key: let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not. Due season is His word, not ours.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shalak (H7993), to cast or fling; nephesh (H5315), life, soul; yasha (H3467), to deliver or save.

expand to see more

Hebrew shalak (H7993) — to cast, to fling; Gideon flung his life out before him.

Hebrew nephesh (H5315) — life, soul, the living self; what was cast.

Hebrew yasha (H3467) — to save, to deliver; what the adventure accomplished for Shechem.

Hebrew gamal (H1580) — to deal out, to requite; the verb of God's rendering to Abimelech.

Hebrew mashal (H4912) — a parable; the form of Jotham's speech about the trees.

Usage

"“my father fought for you, and adventured his life far” — the debt Shechem forgot."

"“he did put his life in his hand, and slew the Philistine” — Jonathan reminding Saul."

"“in due season we shall reap, if we faint not” — the timing that is not ours."
